anchor_quote: zero almost surely, proving the degenerate assertions directly.
text:
The stopping-time hypothesis cannot be omitted. Let the
increments be independent fair signs, so \(\sigma^2=1\), and put
\(T=1\) on \(\{\xi_1=\xi_2\}\) and \(T=2\) otherwise.
This bounded time is not a stopping time. Indeed, \(\xi_1\) is
\(\mathcal F_1\)-measurable and \(\xi_2\) is independent of
\(\mathcal F_1\), so
\(\mathbb P(\xi_1=\xi_2\mid\mathcal F_1)=1/2\) almost surely;
if \(\{T\leq1\}=\{\xi_1=\xi_2\}\) belonged to \(\mathcal F_1\),
this conditional probability would equal its indicator, which
takes only the values \(0\) and \(1\).
On \(\{T=1\}\), \(S_T^2=\xi_1^2=1\); on \(\{T=2\}\),
\(\xi_2=-\xi_1\) and \(S_T=0\). Each event has probability
\(1/2\), so
\[
 \mathbb ES_T^2=\tfrac12,\qquad
 \sigma^2\mathbb ET=\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot2=\tfrac32 .
 \]
The orthogonality step is what fails: \(\mathbf1_{\{T\geq2\}}
=\mathbf1_{\{\xi_2\neq\xi_1\}}\) is not
\(\mathcal F_1\)-measurable, and
\(\mathbb E(\xi_2\mathbf1_{\{T\geq2\}}\mid\mathcal F_1)
 =-\xi_1/2\neq0\).
reason: ED26-P15-CH-optional-stopping-and-random-walks-C009: proves the necessity sentence added to the statement (counterexample E S_T^2=1/2 versus sigma^2 E T=3/2).

anchor_quote:
The equation \(\mathbb Ee^{\theta\xi_1}=1\), with a
nonconstant increment, implies positive probability of both
strictly positive and strictly negative increments.
For if \(\xi_1\geq0\) almost surely, the exponential is at
most one and equality of its mean to one would force
\(\xi_1=0\) almost surely; the nonpositive case is analogous.
Choose \(\delta>0\) with
\(p_\delta=\mathbb P(\xi_1\geq\delta)>0\).
A fixed number \(k\) of such steps, with \(k\delta>b-a\),
forces exit from the interval. Independent disjoint blocks give
\[
 \mathbb P_x(\tau>mk)\leq(1-p_\delta^k)^m,
 \]
so \(\mathbb E_x\tau<\infty\).
text:
The proof of \(\mathbb E_x\tau<\infty\) needs an increment that
is strictly positive with positive probability, so we first
exclude \(\xi_1\leq0\) almost surely.
Suppose \(\xi_1\leq0\) almost surely. Since \(\theta<0\), then
\(\theta\xi_1\geq0\), so the variable
\(W=e^{\theta\xi_1}-1\) is nonnegative almost surely.
By hypothesis \(\mathbb EW=\varphi(\theta)-1=0\).
A nonnegative variable with zero mean vanishes almost surely,
so \(e^{\theta\xi_1}=1\), that is \(\theta\xi_1=0\), almost
surely. As \(\theta\neq0\), this gives \(\xi_1=0\) almost surely,
contradicting the assumption that the increment is nonconstant.
Hence \(\mathbb P(\xi_1>0)>0\).
(The same reasoning applied to \(1-e^{\theta\xi_1}\), which is
nonnegative when \(\xi_1\geq0\), excludes \(\xi_1\geq0\) almost
surely, so negative increments also have positive probability;
that fact is not used below.)

Because \(\{\xi_1>0\}=\bigcup_{r\geq1}\{\xi_1\geq1/r\}\) is an
increasing union, continuity of probability gives some
\(\delta>0\) with
\(p_\delta=\mathbb P(\xi_1\geq\delta)>0\).
Fix an integer \(k\) with \(k\delta>b-a\).
For \(m\geq0\), let \(G_m\) be the event that the \(k\) increments
\(\xi_{mk+1},\ldots,\xi_{mk+k}\) are all at least \(\delta\).
If \(\tau>mk+k\), then \(S_{mk}\) and \(S_{mk+k}\) both lie in
\((a,b)\), so \(S_{mk+k}-S_{mk}<b-a<k\delta\); hence \(G_m\)
fails. Therefore
\(\{\tau>mk\}\subseteq\bigcap_{i=0}^{m-1}G_i^c\).
The blocks are disjoint, so the events \(G_i\) are independent,
each with probability \(p_\delta^k\), and
\[
 \mathbb P_x(\tau>mk)\leq(1-p_\delta^k)^m .
 \]
Since \(\mathbb P_x(\tau>n)\) is nonincreasing in \(n\),
\[
 \mathbb E_x\tau=\sum_{n\geq0}\mathbb P_x(\tau>n)
 \leq k\sum_{m\geq0}\mathbb P_x(\tau>mk)
 \leq k\,p_\delta^{-k}<\infty .
 \]
reason: ED26-P15-CH-optional-stopping-and-random-walks-C020: replaces 'the nonpositive case is analogous' with a written argument that E e^{theta_0 xi_1}=1, theta_0<0 and nonconstant xi_1 exclude xi_1<=0 a.s., and writes out the block bound and the sum giving E_x tau<infinity, on which the overshoot integrability, the exact identity and the lower-exit bound depend.
